1002.title: Who is hearing?
1002.hook: Bassui: ask who is it that hears?
1002.howItsDone: In some Rinzai Zen communities, teachers give students a single question such as Bassui's to carry through sitting and daily work, and check their understanding in private meetings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ikkyu, Crazy Cloud, who laughed at robes and ranks. Your line: the wild monk. Whose puffing up, maybe your own, got a quiet smile? Day one thousand two.

Right now there's a sound somewhere near you. A fridge humming. Traffic. A bird. Someone in the next room. A moment ago you didn't notice it, and now you do. Here's a strange question to put next to that sound. Not what is it, but who is it that's hearing it? It sounds like a riddle for a sleepy afternoon. A Japanese Zen teacher named Bassui made it central to his teaching, and told students to keep asking it until the question itself broke open. Today, Bassui.
screen: `A SOUND, RIGHT NOW.` → `NOT WHAT IS IT.` → `WHO IS HEARING IT?`

segments.voice: Bassui was a Rinzai Zen teacher in Japan who wrote letters and talks for monks, nuns and lay people. Again and again he gave them one question. When you hear a sound, ask: who is hearing? What is it that hears? First, why hearing? Sound is always arriving, so the question is always available. You don't need a temple or a cushion, just ears. Second, what the question is not. Bassui doesn't want an answer like my ears, or my brain, or me. Those are labels. He tells students to turn the attention back from the sound toward the one who hears, and to look there. When they look, they find no object to grab: no shape, no color, nothing to point at. And yet the hearing is plainly happening. Third, the push. When you can't find the hearer, Bassui says, don't give up and don't settle for a clever explanation. Keep asking, more deeply, with your whole body, the way you'd keep searching for something precious you had lost. He describes the questioning growing until it fills everything, and then, at last, breaking open. Fourth, what he says it opens onto: your own mind, which he calls the true master, the Buddha nature that was never born and never dies. Bassui insists it isn't something far away or reserved for monks. It is the one listening to this sentence. Zen schools use questions like this in different ways. Some teachers give a koan to work on; some ask students simply to sit. Bassui's way was this one plain question, carried everywhere.
screen: `BASSUI: ONE QUESTION.` · `WHY HEARING? SOUND IS ALWAYS HERE.` · `LOOK FOR THE HEARER. FIND NO SHAPE.` · `KEEP ASKING, WITH YOUR WHOLE BODY.` · then, large: `WHO IS HEARING?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: listen, and ask who hears. Sit still and let the sounds come to you. Don't name them. Just let them arrive: near, far, loud, soft. Then, gently, ask inside: who is hearing this? Don't answer with a word. Turn the attention back from the sound toward wherever the hearing is happening, and look. If you find nothing to hold, that's fine. Stay with the not-finding. When the mind drifts off, let the next sound call you back, and ask again. The bell holds the time.
Bassui. The Zen teacher who told students, when a sound comes, to turn from it and ask who is hearing, and keep looking. Today's word.
Your line: stay with the not-finding. Today, when a sound interrupts you, a phone, a horn, a kettle, let it be a bell, and ask the question once. Day one thousand two.

1003.title: The unborn
1003.hook: Bankei taught ordinary people: you already have the unborn Buddha-mind
1003.howItsDone: Zen students and teachers read Bankei's recorded talks and point to the unborn mind in everyday life; his way is often taught without koans, as trusting the mind that is already working.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bassui's question: when a sound comes, who is hearing? Your line: stay with the not-finding. Which sound became a bell for you? Day one thousand three.

A man comes to a Zen teacher with a confession. I was born with a short temper, he says. It's just how I am. How do I fix it? The teacher looks interested. That's remarkable, he says. Show it to me. The man says he can't, not right now. It only comes out sometimes, when something sets it off. Then, says the teacher, it isn't something you were born with. You make it, on the spot. The teacher was Bankei, and he told plain stories like this to ordinary people. Today, the unborn.
screen: `I WAS BORN THIS WAY.` → `SHOW IT TO ME.` → `YOU MAKE IT ON THE SPOT.`

segments.voice: Bankei was a Japanese Rinzai Zen teacher, and his teaching fits in a sentence. Everyone already has the Buddha-mind, and it is unborn. First, unborn. Bankei means a mind that was never produced, never put together, so it can never fall apart. It's what's here before you start building moods and grudges and stories. He says everything is handled perfectly well by it, without your adding anything. Second, ordinary people. Bankei spoke in everyday Japanese, not in the scholar's Chinese of the sutras. Records of his talks show farmers, townspeople, women and men, monks and lay people coming to listen. He mostly skipped the old koan stories and talked about their actual lives: anger, worry, sleepiness, the neighbors. Third, how the unborn gets lost. In the temper story, nobody is born angry. Something happens, you want your own way, and you turn the unborn mind into a fighting mind. Bankei calls that trading the Buddha-mind for something smaller. Don't fight the anger with more effort, he says. Just don't make it. Stay unborn. Fourth, trust. Bankei was wary of teachers who told students to strain and grind for awakening. So his advice is gentle: you already have it. Stop swapping it for something else. On an ordinary day, the unborn sounds like this: the kettle clicks off, and you just hear it. Someone cuts in line, and for one beat, before the story starts, there's only seeing.
screen: `THE BUDDHA-MIND IS UNBORN.` · `PLAIN WORDS FOR ORDINARY PEOPLE.` · `NOBODY IS BORN ANGRY.` · `YOU ALREADY HAVE IT.` · then, large: `STAY UNBORN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: trust your ordinary mind. Sit however is comfortable. Don't try to make anything happen. Notice that seeing is already happening without your effort: light, shapes, the room. Feeling is already happening: the seat, the air, the breath. You didn't build any of it. When a thought starts building something, a plan, a complaint, a worry, notice the building, and don't add the next brick. Come back to what's already working fine on its own. Nothing to earn here. The bell holds the time.
The unborn. Bankei's word for the Buddha-mind everyone already has, never produced, so it never falls apart. Today's word.
Your line: the kettle clicks off. Today, when irritation starts to rise, catch the beat before it, and see if you can leave the irritation unmade. Day one thousand three.

1004.title: The old pond
1004.hook: Basho's poem of a frog jumping into an old pond: a haiku as a moment of attention
1004.howItsDone: People in Japan and around the world write haiku as a way of paying attention, and some Zen communities and poetry groups hold walks where each person writes a short poem about something seen or heard on the way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bankei and the unborn, the mind nobody has to build. Your line: the kettle clicks off. Did you catch the beat before an irritation, and leave it unmade? Day one thousand four.

Furuike ya, kawazu tobikomu, mizu no oto. That's the whole poem, in Japanese. Said slowly, it barely fills a breath. In plain English it comes out something like: the old pond. A frog jumps in. The sound of water. No moral. No feeling announced. No sunset, no heartbreak. A pond, a frog, a splash. It was written by Matsuo Basho, a Japanese poet who walked the roads with very little and wrote as he went. Today, Basho.
screen: `FURUIKE YA.` → `A POND, A FROG, A SPLASH.` → `MATSUO BASHO.`

segments.voice: Basho wasn't a monastery teacher, but tradition says he practiced Zen with a priest, and his poems are often read alongside Zen. Here's why. First, the stillness. Furuike, the old pond. Not a lively pond, not a pretty one. Old. Still. The poem starts with a quiet so deep it has gone a little mossy. The little word ya after it is a pause, like a breath held: the old pond, and. Second, the event. Kawazu tobikomu, a frog jumps in. Something small and alive breaks the stillness. It's not a heron or a dragon. A frog, an ordinary creature at the edge of a pond. Third, the sound. Mizu no oto, the sound of water. Notice the poem doesn't say the frog is beautiful, or that the speaker felt peace. It just stops at the sound, and lets the sound be the whole thing. And then, implied, the quiet comes back, and it's a different quiet, because now you heard it break. Readers have taken this poem in more than one way. Some hear impermanence: the splash, and gone. Some hear the stillness and the movement as one thing, the way Dogen spoke of being-time. Some hear a man simply paying attention so completely that nothing extra gets in. That last reading points at what a haiku can do. It can be less a poem about a moment than a moment, set down so cleanly that someone else can step into it, long after, and hear the water.
screen: `THE OLD POND: STILLNESS.` · `A FROG JUMPS IN.` · `THE SOUND OF WATER, AND IT STOPS.` · `A MOMENT, NOT A POEM ABOUT ONE.` · then, large: `MIZU NO OTO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: write one three-line moment, in your head first. Sit, and let the breath slow. Then look and listen for one small thing that is really happening right now. A car door. A cup on the table. Light on a wall. Find the still thing, the moving thing and the sound or detail that lands. Three short lines. No feelings announced, no lesson. Just the thing, the way Basho let the frog be a frog. Say the lines silently once. Then let them go, and keep listening. The bell holds the time.
Basho. The Japanese poet whose haiku of the old pond, a frog, and a splash became a model of pure attention. Today's word.
Your line: the sound of water. Today, when you run a tap or hear rain, stop for one breath and let it be the whole poem. Day one thousand four.

1005.title: "Is that so?"
1005.hook: the story of Hakuin, falsely blamed for a baby, who says "is that so?" and cares for the child
1005.howItsDone: Zen teachers and Buddhist writers retell the Is that so? story as a teaching on equanimity, and Buddhist teachers present praise and blame alike as passing conditions, an old theme in the Buddha's teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Basho's old pond: a frog jumps in, the sound of water, nothing added. Your line: the sound of water. Did a tap or the rain get to be the whole poem? Day one thousand five.

Angry parents are pounding on a temple door. Their unmarried daughter is pregnant, and when they pressed her to name the father, she named the respected Zen master who lives in the village temple. The whole neighborhood has heard. The parents shout their accusation in his face. The master listens, and says three words: Is that so? That's all. No denial. No speech. The story is told about Hakuin, a Japanese Zen teacher, and today we follow it to the end.
screen: `ANGRY PARENTS AT THE DOOR.` → `THEY BLAME THE MASTER.` → `IS THAT SO?`

segments.voice: First, a word about where this comes from. It's a story people tell about Hakuin, and nobody can say whether it happened as told. But it has traveled because it shows something clearly. Here's how it goes on. When the baby is born, the family brings the infant to Hakuin and leaves the child with him. You did this, so you raise it. Hakuin's reputation is gone. People stop coming to hear him. He says, Is that so? And he takes the baby. He begs milk from neighbors and whatever else the child needs, and he looks after the little one with care. Time passes. Then the young mother can't bear it anymore. She tells her parents the truth: the real father is a young man who works in the fish market. The parents rush back to the temple, ashamed. They apologize, over and over, and ask for the child back. Hakuin hands the baby over, and says: Is that so? Notice what the three words are doing. The first time, they aren't agreement, and they aren't a lie. They're a refusal to fight about his own name while a baby needs looking after. The second time, they aren't triumph. No I told you so. Praise and blame come and go, and he treats them the same way, like weather. And through all of it, the one thing that doesn't change is the care. The story isn't asking anyone to accept every false charge in silence. Some readers hear it as a story about ego: how little Hakuin needed to be seen as right. Others hear it about attention: whatever people were saying, he kept his eyes on the child.
screen: `A STORY PEOPLE TELL.` · `HE TAKES THE BABY, AND CARES.` · `THE TRUTH COMES OUT.` · `PRAISE AND BLAME, LIKE WEATHER.` · then, large: `IS THAT SO?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: answer one accusation calmly, here, in rehearsal. Sit, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind a small criticism you've heard lately, fair or unfair. Not the worst one. A small one. Notice what rises in the body: heat, a tight jaw, a speech getting ready. Let all that be there. Then, silently, try Hakuin's words: is that so? Feel the space they open, before any reply. You can still answer later, and correct the record if you need to. For now, just breathe in the space. The bell holds the time.
Hakuin. The Zen teacher the story gives three words, is that so, for blame and praise alike, while he keeps caring for the child. Today's word.
Your line: blame and praise, like weather. Today, when someone tells you what you are, good or bad, try saying to yourself, is that so, before you answer. Day one thousand five.

1006.title: Hakuin's cure
1006.hook: Hakuin's "Zen sickness" and the butter-ball meditation he learned from a hermit
1006.howItsDone: Some Zen teachers pass on Hakuin's soft-butter method and his practice of settling attention in the lower belly, especially for students who are tense or overstraining, and people read his account in Idle Talk on a Night Boat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the story of Hakuin and the baby, and three words for blame and praise alike. Your line: blame and praise, like weather. Did those words come first, before a reply? Day one thousand six.

Hakuin, the same Zen teacher from yesterday's story, wrote about a time when practice made him sick. As a young monk he threw himself at it, sitting, straining, pushing day and night. Then, in his own telling, his body turned on him. His head burned, his legs felt like ice, his ears rang, he was anxious and couldn't rest, and doctors couldn't help. He called it Zen sickness. So Hakuin went looking for a hermit in the mountains. Today, Hakuin's cure.
screen: `STRAINING DAY AND NIGHT.` → `ZEN SICKNESS.` → `A HERMIT IN THE MOUNTAINS.`

segments.voice: The account comes from a short work of Hakuin's, often called Idle Talk on a Night Boat. First, the hermit. Hakuin says he climbed into the hills near Kyoto to find a recluse named Hakuyu, who lived in a cave. Hakuyu listened, and told him the trouble wasn't that he'd practiced too little. He'd pushed all the energy up into his head, and it needed to come down. Second, settling low. Hakuyu taught him to bring his attention and breath down into the lower belly, below the navel, and to rest it there, especially at night, lying down. Third, the butter, the image at the center of it. Imagine, Hakuyu said, a lump of soft, fragrant butter resting on the crown of your head. Slowly it warms and begins to melt. It trickles down over the head, the face and shoulders, through the chest and the belly, down the back and the legs, all the way to the soles of the feet, soothing everything it touches as it goes. Fourth, the result. In Hakuin's telling he practiced this patiently, and over time he recovered, and he went on to teach it to his own students. Readers differ about the story. Some take the hermit at face value. Others think Hakuin shaped the account to make a teaching memorable. Either way, the point he draws is plain: strain for awakening with only your head, and the body pays. Bring the warmth back down. And one honest note: this is a meditation, not a medical treatment. Hakuin's lesson is about balance in practice.
screen: `HAKUYU, THE HERMIT.` · `BRING IT DOWN TO THE BELLY.` · `THE BUTTER MELTS, HEAD TO FEET.` · `BALANCE, NOT STRAIN.` · then, large: `THE BUTTER MELTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: imagine warmth melting down your body. Sit or lie down, comfortably. Let the breath settle low in the belly. Now picture something soft and warm resting on the top of your head. Butter, as Hakuyu said, or warm honey, or sunlight, whatever feels kind. Let it slowly melt. Feel it ease over the forehead and the jaw, soften the shoulders, warm the chest, settle in the belly, and flow down the legs to the feet. Wherever it meets tightness, let it take its time. Then rest in the warmth that's left. The bell holds the time.
Hakuin's cure. The soft-butter meditation he says he learned from the hermit Hakuyu, bringing warmth and attention down from the head to the feet. Today's word.
Your line: the butter melts. Tonight, lying down, let warmth melt once from the crown of your head to your feet before you sleep. Day one thousand six.

1007.title: Ryokan and the thief
1007.hook: the poet-monk wishes he could give the thief the moon in his window
1007.carry: I wish I could give the moon
1007.howItsDone: Ryokan's poems and the stories told about him are read in Zen communities and beyond as pictures of a simple, generous life, and Buddhist teaching names giving, dana, as a practice to cultivate.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hakuin's cure: the soft lump of butter on the crown of the head, melting down through the body. Your line was the butter melts. Where did something soften? Day one thousand seven.

A small hut on a hillside in Japan. It belongs to an old monk who owns almost nothing. One night a thief slips in, searches every corner, and finds nothing worth taking. Then the monk comes home and catches him. The thief freezes. The monk, the story goes, isn't angry. He's sorry. You came all this way, he says, and there's nothing here for you. So he takes off his own clothes and hands them over. The thief grabs them and runs into the dark. The monk sits down in his empty doorway and looks up at the moon. The monk was Ryokan, and this story is today's word.
screen: `A THIEF IN AN EMPTY HUT.` → `THE MONK GIVES HIM HIS CLOTHES.` → `THE MOON OVERHEAD.`

segments.voice: First, where the story comes from. It's a story people tell about Ryokan, a Zen monk and poet who lived simply, begging for his food in the villages nearby. Tradition remembers him in a hut with a begging bowl rather than at the head of a temple. The thief story fits everything else people remember about him. Second, the gift. Ryokan doesn't defend what little he has, and he doesn't lecture. He sees a man who came looking for something and is about to leave with nothing, and that seems to bother him more than the loss. His clothes are the only thing in the hut worth giving, so he gives them. Buddhist teaching calls giving dana, and treats it as a practice, not only a kindness: something you do on purpose, again and again, until the hand opens more easily. Third, the moon. After the thief is gone, tradition says, Ryokan wrote a very short poem. In plain English it runs something like this: the thief left it behind, the moon in my window. He wished, the story goes, that he could have given the man the moon too. In the poem, the one thing worth having couldn't be carried off. It was still there, shining in the window. Fourth, why this matters on an ordinary day. A thief may never come to your door. Small takings do: a seat, a parking space, the credit for an idea. Ryokan's story doesn't ask how to get it back. It asks what's still in the window that nobody could take, and whether you could give a little more than was taken.
screen: `A STORY TOLD ABOUT RYOKAN.` · `HE GIVES THE THIEF HIS CLOTHES.` · `THE MOON LEFT IN THE WINDOW.` · `WHAT NOBODY COULD TAKE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give one thing away, first in your mind. Settle, and breathe. Look around at what's near you, or bring your room to mind. Choose one thing you could give away today: a book, a jacket, an hour of your time, a kind word you've been holding back. Notice the small tug of wanting to keep it. Don't fight the tug. Just breathe with it. Then, if you like, decide who it's for. Let your eyes rest on something open, a window, the sky, a light, something nobody can take from you. The bell holds the time.
Ryokan. The poet-monk who gave a thief his clothes and wished he could give him the moon as well. Today's word.
Your line: I wish I could give the moon. Today, give away one thing freely, with no note attached and no thanks expected. Day one thousand seven.

1008.title: Ryokan plays
1008.hook: Ryokan plays hide and seek with village children till after dark
1008.howItsDone: Ryokan's poems about children and play are read in Zen communities and in Japanese schools and homes, and his story is told as a picture of practice that includes simple joy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ryokan and the thief, the monk who gave away his clothes and kept the moon. Your line was I wish I could give the moon. What did you give away? Day one thousand eight.
screen: `I WISH I COULD GIVE THE MOON.`

segments.voice: Late afternoon in a village. A group of children run up to an old monk with a begging bowl and shout his name. Not to ask for a blessing. To ask him to play. He sets the bowl down. They play ball, then hide and seek, and when it's his turn to hide he crawls into a pile of straw in a field and goes perfectly still. The children search. It gets dark. They go home for supper and forget all about him. The next morning, the story goes, a farmer comes to move the straw and finds the monk still there. Shh, the monk whispers. The children will find me. Today's word: Ryokan plays.
screen: `THE CHILDREN WANT TO PLAY.` → `HE HIDES IN THE STRAW.` → `SHH. THEY'LL FIND ME.`

segments.voice: First, how the story reaches us. Like the thief story, it's a story people tell about Ryokan. Versions differ on where he hid; the monk stays the same. Second, play as practice. Ryokan's poems, as they've come down to us, keep returning to children, to a ball, to a spring day that ends too soon. Tradition says he carried a cloth handball in his sleeve. For him, playing doesn't seem to have been time stolen from practice. It was a place practice showed up: full attention, no score worth keeping, no reputation to protect. Third, still hiding. Why stay all night? Some readers hear a holy fool, a man too simple to notice the game was over. Others hear faithfulness: he gave his word to the game, and he kept it. Others hear complete absorption, so present to hiding that nobody was left inside to give up. The story doesn't choose for you. Fourth, the week behind us. It's been a week of teachers from Japan. Bassui asked who is hearing. Bankei pointed to the unborn mind, already here. Basho heard the sound of water when a frog jumped into an old pond. Hakuin, blamed for a baby that wasn't his, said is that so, and taught the butter that melts. Ryokan gave away his clothes and kept the moon. And today he's in the straw, still hiding, waiting for the children to come back.
